A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same specialization-after-generalization study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching the relocated MoE results and experimental details.

before.justification: Sections 3–4 and Appendices D–E report original SAE analyses, MNIST and ImageNet experiments, language-model evaluations on the Pile, and MoE comparisons.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds neighborhood accuracy measurements and an end-to-end versus last-layer TTT experiment on MNIST.

M1.justification: The principal neighborhood-based TTT procedures, SAE construction, adaptive masking objective, and language-model LoRA adaptation remain unchanged. V3's full-model MNIST adaptation is introduced as an auxiliary comparison and ablation; it does not replace the studied last-layer procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use MNIST, ImageNet-1K, and the same 17-subdataset Pile configuration. Added model sizes, adaptation controls, and evaluation on existing adaptation neighborhoods do not introduce different datasets, populations, domains, or task requirements.

E2.justification: V3 adds end-to-end TTT as a comparator to last-layer TTT and global training on MNIST (Appendix D.2, Figure 7). Existing majority-voting, sparse-concept TTT, and MoE comparisons remain. The Bertolissi et al. MoE comparison moves to Appendix F.5 rather than being removed.

E3.justification: MNIST scaling expands from ten to twelve model sizes, extending the documented maximum from 40,818 to 85,866 parameters. Appendix D.2 adds full-model adaptation with separately tuned learning rates, epochs, and neighborhood sizes. ImageNet learning-rate entries also change, such as 3e-4 to 3.5e-4 for the 500-unit MLP (v1 Table 7; v3 Table 8); these reported revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The new MNIST ablation tests whether restricting adaptation to the classification head materially affects the scaling findings, reporting nearly identical errors for full-model and head-only TTT. Table 2 adds neighborhood-fit measurements to the local-versus-global analysis. Existing masking, neighborhood-size, and cross-entropy analyses remain; the width-based Figure 6 is a redisplay, not an independent new analysis.

E5.justification: The reporting practices remain bootstrap standard errors, 90% bootstrap confidence intervals, and five-seed MNIST scaling with 200 bootstrap iterations per seed. The added end-to-end experiment also uses five seeds. Additional entries follow existing practices without an established increase in repeated runs or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: V3 Table 2 adds TTT neighborhood accuracies of 100.00±0.00 for MNIST and 95.19±0.00 for ImageNet. Existing TTT test-point accuracies remain 99.01±0.10 and 79.39±0.18, respectively; the neighborhood measurements are separate outcomes. V3 also adds two MNIST scaling configurations and the finding that full-model and last-layer TTT have nearly identical errors. The principal scaling trends remain.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds a constant upper bound on the local coefficient norms ||w_i||_2. Appendix C.4 revises the Hermite/Ornstein–Uhlenbeck argument, changes the sample upper-bound inequality, and reverses the stated Gaussian Index Model comparison from easier to harder. These are localized mathematical revisions to the auxiliary hardness result; assumptions A1–A9, the TTT recovery bound, and the global interference formula remain.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claims: TTT specializes existing concepts, can improve in-distribution predictions in underparameterized models, and has diminishing benefits as capacity increases. The introduction's effective-underparameterization wording clarifies an existing claim. The conclusion changes future-work emphasis without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly warns that large label noise or violations of the hypotheses may impair TTT (Section 5.1, footnote 7). It interprets the new MNIST ablation as supporting head-only adaptation. Appendix A.1 also expands the distinction between its function class and globally Lipschitz functions, explaining the role of behavior at cell boundaries.

D1.justification: V3 supplies end-to-end TTT hyperparameters, settings for larger MNIST models, ImageNet parameter counts, and broader validation-based tuning disclosures. The code link is retained in Appendix F. However, new ImageNet prose describes 600 neighbors and learning rate 0.02 as applicable across scales, while Table 9 retains 100 neighbors and 0.005 for MLP heads, leaving that statement's scope unclear.

R1.justification: V3 adds Bommasani et al. (2021) for foundation-model framing, Zhang et al. (2025) on TTT, and Belkin et al. (2019) and Frei et al. (2022) for implicit-bias discussion. The central positioning against non-parametric explanations remains. Publication updates for already cited works do not constitute additional research coverage.

P1.justification: V3 edits the introduction and several experimental explanations, reorganizes the auxiliary hardness discussion, adds an experimental-results appendix, and consolidates the MoE discussion with its implementation details in Appendix F.5. It also removes the acknowledgments. The main section sequence and overall narrative remain recognizable.

P2.justification: V3 revises Figure 4's vision axes to show parameter counts, adds a width-based redisplay in Figure 6, and introduces the end-to-end comparison Figure 7 and its hyperparameter table. Table 2 gains a neighborhood column, and several settings tables expand. The MoE plot moves from main-text Figure 6 to appendix Figure 9; the retained loss plots also receive parameter-count axes.

improvement.justification: The new MNIST end-to-end control directly tests the reliance on head-only adaptation, strengthening support for that experimental design choice. Neighborhood-fit measurements and fuller hyperparameter documentation also make the evidence easier to assess. These gains are limited to the retained research scope, and the new ambiguity between ImageNet's broadly stated settings and its MLP table offsets some of the reproducibility benefit.
